text: Scripting & Application Development already covered how one scoped application isolates itself with its own sys_scope namespace. This lesson asks a different question — the one that only shows up once an organization has built dozens of them.

That earlier course taught the mechanics of one scoped application. This lesson asks how many scoped applications an instance should actually have, and where the boundaries between them should fall — a question about the whole portfolio, not any single app.

Too many narrowly-scoped applications means more separate upgrade-testing efforts and more cross-app integration points to manage, often for splits that don't reflect any real organizational boundary at all. Too few, overly broad scopes create genuine coupling instead: a bug fixed in one unrelated feature can break every other feature bundled into the same giant scope, because they all deploy and roll back together.

The practical guidance that holds up at scale: a scope boundary should follow a real functional and ownership boundary, the edge where one team builds, tests, and deploys independently of another. Two features owned by the same team on the same release cadence probably belong in one scope. A separate team with its own release calendar deserves its own scope, regardless of how small it is.

Once an organization has more than a couple of interdependent scoped applications, dependency discipline becomes real architectural work. Pinning a dependency to a specific Application Repository version, rather than always consuming the latest, means a breaking change published inside one app doesn't silently break another app that depends on it.

That discipline is what lets many teams move fast inside their own scope without breaking everyone else's, at enterprise scale. Next: the Platform Architecture Lab, a worked scenario applying instance strategy, Domain Separation, and scope boundaries together.
